You seem knowledgeable about nuclear. Could you please give your opinion on my question about what would happen to nuclear power plants in case of a societal collapse.

I'm only as knowledgeable about nuclear plants as the next random engineer off the street. The answer to your question requires a bit of speculation and supposition.

So the government collapses and anarchy reigns. Wide-spread chaos and violence erupt as factions popup and fight to control territory and resources. What happens to the reactors can be one of a few things.

Nuclear reactors have to be maintained by whatever staff is currently available on site. Usually that consists of a few operating technicians, a supervising engineer, maintenance staff and miscellaneous staff, in addition to security personnel, all of which operate in shifts.

So in this situation, the operating staff at the reactor were all killed (say someone raided the site), Leaving the control rods in their steady-state position. In this situation the plant will continue to produce electricity (assuming no systems were damaged in the assault on the site) until either:

A) The reactor is designed to automatically shut itself down if left unattended. With the reactor shut down, 90% of the fissile reaction has been reduced, the power production is brought down to a minimum. In this state the reactor can sit for an indeterminate amount of time. At some point a problem is likely to occur, but that'll depend on the reactor design, materials used, operation, etc, etc. I can safely say that a reactor in shut down state is pretty much safe for at least a couple years. To the best of my knowledge no reaction has ever been put into such a situation before.

B) The reactor is successfully SCRAMed by the staff, then we're back to A.

C) Someone prevents the reactor from automatically shutting down and the coolant in the reactor reaches a level where the fuel rods are exposed to air at which point the rods will begin to heat excessively and boil off the remaining coolant, leaving the reaction to "run away" until the reactor melts or explodes. It will then proceed uncontrolled in a fashion similar to Chernobyl, with lots of fire and radioactive ash until becomes a radioactive crater that kills everything within a hundred miles (depending on prevailing winds)

This could be days to a couple weeks before it occurs. Depends on extenuating circumstances with regards to the coolant supply.

D) Same scenario as B but the reaction falls out of steady-state, and the control rods are not adjusted to compensate (or fully retracted), resulting in another run away reaction, similarly leading to a meltdown.

This could be a matter of hours.

E) The coolant in the spent fuel rod pool falls enough to expose the rods to the air, at which point thing like hydrogen gas are released and build up in the roof of the containment shed, and a Fukushima happens. However since no one is responding to halt the crisis the subsequent explosion, or fires initiated by it, of the containment shed could damage the reactor, and then a potential meltdown could occur. The spent fuel rods melt through the containment pool floor and eventually find their way into the water table. If no explosion occurs and the pressure is vented to the atmosphere, then a cloud of radioactive gas is released rendering the facility and surrounding area uninhabitable.

Could be days or weeks or even hours. Really depends on how fast coolant is lost from the pool with out it being resupplied.

I'm sure there's some other scenarios which could happen, such a subsystem failure or damage to the facility causing a problem, but these are pretty much the ultimate failure state of the reactor. Most problems that could occur, left unchecked, would result in one of the latter three cases assuming the reactor is unable to be shut down.

Probability-wise the reactor would be shut down or SCRAMed immediately in the event of an attack, leaving only E as a probable situation. There's literally a button in the control room which initiates emergency shutdowns, and it takes only a few seconds for SCRAM process to occur.

More likely scenarios is the reactor facility is taken over by a faction and the staff press-ganged into permanent servitude until they train up replacements. Or reactors will be completely left alone because only the most moronic of individuals would attempt to storm one due to inherent dangers of mucking about haphazardly in nuclear science.

Even more likely in the event the Federal Government collapses, each state will simply assume independent behavior and maintain its previous governmental procedures and little will change (apart from econ). It really depends on the details of the destabilizing factors and there's just too many to account for. Either way there are lots of cases and contingencies planned for by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and with the number of safety systems in each reactor, there's not likely many of them that are going to meltdown.
After a reactor is SCRAMed, how long would it take for it to cool down enough so E couldn't happen?
